thread.title: Oil turns higher as supply relief offsets stock-market drop

author: Rachel Koning Beals
title: Oil turns higher as supply relief offsets stock-market drop
text:
Oil prices edged higher Thursday, getting a boost as separate surveys revealed monthly declines in crude output from major producers, but the drop in the stock market continued to fuel investor unease.
Members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries produced 32.68 million barrels of oil a day in December, down 460,000 barrels a day from a month earlier, according to a Reuters survey released Thursday . Separately, a Bloomberg survey showed OPEC output down by 530,000 barrels to 32.6 million barrels a day last month. Both surveys pegged the monthly declines as the biggest since January 2017.
The output declines came ahead of the reduction of 1.2 million barrels a day from October 2018 levels pledged by OPEC and nonmember producers, including Russia, that became effective at the start of the new year.
However, Thursday’s “volatility across risk assets, including energy, is growth related and fears of a slowing global economy continue to be a major headwind on oil from a demand standpoint,” said Tyler Richey, co-editor of the Sevens Report.
Against that backdrop, West Texas Intermediate crude for February delivery CLG9, +0.30% added 24 cents, or 0.5%, to $46.78 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, after an earlier decline to a low at $45.35. Front-month WTI crude futures dropped by 24.8% in 2018, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
The global benchmark, March Brent crude UK:LCOG9 meanwhile, added 45 cents, or 0.8%, to $55.36 a barrel on ICE Futures Europe, following earlier lows under $54. The international benchmark finished last year with a loss of 19.5%.

“Oil is due for a bounce as futures are oversold but without a notable catalyst, and a rebound in stocks, it will be hard for WTI to rally beyond resistance in the low $50s,” said Richey.
On Wednesday, prices for both benchmark crudes settled at two-week highs after a reported drop in December crude exports emerged from Saudi Arabia .
Oil’s upside has been limited in part by concerns about the global economy, especially after the latest round of worrying statistics out of China, and its potential impact on demand for crude. Demand is also in question as wealth is wiped out of stock markets, the latest blow due to a sales warning from Apple AAPL, -9.30%
AAPL, -9.30% AAPL, -9.30% Meanwhile, major crude producers, including the U.S. and Russia, continued to ramp up output in the second half of 2018. The U.S. Energy Information Administration forecasts American output will rise to 12.1 million barrels a day in 2019, up 1.2 million barrels a day from the previous year.
Data “showing some global producers finished the year pumping at record levels with forecasts for 2019 still pointing to further output growth, especially in the U.S. … further raises concerns about a [supply] surplus lasting into the new year,” said Richey.
Rounding out the action in the energy market, February gasoline RBG9, +0.82% traded at $1.338 a gallon, up 0.9% on Nymex, while February heating oil HOG9, +1.51% added 1.4% to $1.724 a gallon.
February natural gas NGG19, -0.74% fell 0.4% to $2.947 per million British thermal units. It trades more than 10% lower week to date.
On Friday morning, the Energy Information Administration will release its weekly data on U.S. natural-gas supplies, followed by the weekly report on domestic petroleum stockpiles. Both are delayed this week because of Tuesday’s New Year’s Day holiday.
The American Petroleum Institute, a trade group, will release its weekly domestic petroleum inventory report later Thursday, which has also been delayed due to the holiday.
Analysts polled by S&P Global Platts expected the EIA to report a fall of 1.3 million barrels in crude supplies for the week ended Dec. 28, along with increases of 1.6 million barrels each for gasoline and distillate inventories.
